newsitem.title: SPAIN: Madrid airport restores calm after near disasters.
newsitem.headline: Madrid airport restores calm after near disasters.

text.p: Madrid's main airport recovered its composure and returned to business as usual on Sunday after one of the worst weeks in its history in which it staggered from one near disaster to another.
Rocked by a fire which forced a five-hour shut-down on Tuesday, Madrid's Barajas airport soon found itself facing another close shave on Thursday after an aircraft skidded off the runway.
"Everything has returned to normal now and there have been no incidents since Thursday. There are no cancellations today and only small delays," an airport official told Reuters.

The airport received a barage of criticism as it struggled to deal with this week's incidents, prompting calls for a shake-up of its safety procedures and immediate action to relieve congestion at the over-stretched airport.

"It's inconceivable that the infrastructure of an airport as important as Barajas is insufficient to cope with any emergency and that we had to close the airport in order to put out a fire and restore the electricity supply," said Fernando Pina, chairman of Spain's airport authority AENA.
The fire, caused by workmen who drilled through an electrical cable, highlighted the absence of an effective procedure to deal with such emergencies.
"The security systems at Barajas are a joke, they are like third world systems," said Development Minister Rafael Arias Salgado shortly afterwards.
Although the fire was extinguished by midday on Tuesday, it later broke out again forcing the airport to shut down for the first time in its history when the runway lights failed.
Efforts to recover from the resulting chaos on Wednesday were aggravated by a 24-hour strike by public sector workers and a series of electricity cuts.
And as the airport paused for breath on Thursday it again found itself wiping sweat from its brow after an Iberia aircraft slid off the end of the runway with 103 passengers on board.
After an emergency evacuation, passengers said they had to wait beside the runway for fifteen minutes in heavy rain until the emergency services arrived.
Furthermore, it took over 15 hours to clear the aircraft from the end of the runway aggravating delays and cancellations.
No one was injured in either of the incidents but airport officials emerged red-faced. AENA reacted with a proposal to improve safety and ease overcrowding.
"We have put in place a shock plan from today...so that this situation can never be repeated," Pina said on Wednesday.
AENA met with Salgado on Saturday to discuss the plan which includes preparation of a former U.S military base at nearby Torrejon to relieve Barajas of some of its commercial flights.
Barajas, Spain's busiest airport with around 20 million passengers a year, has been struggling with an increasing amount of air traffic in recent months.
A contract to build a third runway has been awarded but construction will take almost two years.
Major airlines are demanding compensation for this week's mayhem. On Tuesday alone, 300 flights were cancelled.
